title: Apple Beat on Everything. The Stock Crashed Anyway.
subtitle: Record revenue, a blowout iPhone quarter, and an EPS beat — yet Apple just suffered its worst post-earnings day in 13 years and lost its crown as the world's most valuable company. The culprits: a guidance miss and a '100-year flood' in memory pricing.
summary: Apple posted its best June quarter ever — $109.42B in revenue and a $2.02 EPS beat — and the stock still crashed, erasing roughly $360B in market value. The culprit: soft September guidance and a memory shortage that is about to squeeze iPhone margins to levels unseen in a decade.

image.alt: Apple faces massive post-earnings selloff as memory shortage threatens iPhone margins

bodyHtml:
Apple just reported the best June quarter in its history. Revenue of $109.42 billion, up 16.4% year over year. Earnings per share of $2.02, blowing past the $1.89 consensus. Net income of $29.79 billion. And the stock suffered its worst post-earnings day since January 2013, with roughly $360 billion in market value erased in a single session. Read that again: Apple beat on the top line, beat on the bottom line, and the market responded by treating the report like a disaster. That disconnect is the entire story of this quarter — and it was entirely self-inflicted.

The numbers were, on their face, spectacular. iPhone revenue hit $54.25 billion, up 22%, powered by the strongest product cycle in years. Mac revenue climbed 29% to $10.35 billion. But Services — Apple's supposed moat and margin sanctuary — grew just 12% to $30.74 billion and missed analyst estimates. That miss matters more than any beat, because Services is the crown jewel of the Apple bull case: recurring, high-margin, sticky. When that wobbles, the whole narrative wobbles with it.

Wall Street's verdict was brutal. The stock tumbled to levels last seen months ago, wiping out roughly $360 billion of market value — from about $4.90 trillion to $4.54 trillion — and ceding the title of the world's most valuable company back to Nvidia. Investors didn't have to squint to find the culprit. It was guidance, and it was ugly.

For the September quarter, Apple guided revenue growth of 9% to 11%, versus the 12% the Street expected. Gross margin guidance of 47% to 48% came in below the 48% plus that analysts were modeling. The market can forgive a lot when a company beats the quarter it just reported. It rarely forgives a company that says the next quarter will be worse than expected — especially when it sounds like an excuse you've heard before. Except this time, it's real.

The excuse is memory. DRAM, NAND, and HBM — the silicon inside everything from iPhones to AI data centers — has been devoured by the AI buildout, and prices have roughly doubled over the past year. Tim Cook, in his final earnings call as CEO, called it a "100-year flood on memory pricing" and warned of "very significant supply constraints." The AI boom that made Apple's rivals unstoppable has become the single biggest threat to Apple's margins.

The consequences are already visible. Apple raised Mac and iPad prices by 17% to 25% in June, and the iPhone 18 Pro is expected to start at $1,299 — about $200 more than its predecessor. Jefferies estimates that memory costs alone could shave iPhone gross margin from around 38% to roughly 34.5% in the second half of the year. That is the kind of compression Apple hasn't had to think about in a decade, and it's not a one-quarter problem: memory pricing is still climbing.

KeyBank laid out the bear case in its bleakest form: price hikes slow unit growth, slower unit growth slows the installed base, and a slower installed base slows Services. Apple is being forced to choose between margin today and users tomorrow — and the choice it's being pushed into is the one that hurts the long-term franchise. Cook acknowledged the tension on the call:

"We're having an incredibly strong product cycle beyond our expectations, and the supply chain just fundamentally has less flexibility in it to meet the high levels of demand."

Then came the kicker:

"If you look beyond September, we see the market pricing for memory continuing to increase, which could drive an increasing impact on our business."

There's a deeply human subplot here. This was Cook's last earnings call before handing the keys to John Ternus on September 1. A thirteen-year CEO run ends with the stock suffering its worst post-earnings day since 2013, a quarter of historic demand, and a supply chain that can't keep up with it. Ternus inherits a company that is simultaneously firing on all cylinders and walking into a margin headwind it cannot control. The transition could not be more awkwardly timed.

Here's the takeaway: Apple's problem was never demand. It's that the AI boom — the very force lifting the entire market — has turned memory into the new oil, and Apple doesn't own the wells. The company will pass the costs to customers, and customers will pay, because the iPhone remains the iPhone. But the era of Apple as an untouchable margin fortress is over, at least for now. Watch the December quarter like a hawk. If memory keeps climbing and Apple keeps raising prices, the KeyBank bear case stops being a scenario and starts being a forecast.

Disclosure: The Signal holds no position in AAPL. Positions may change. This is not financial advice.
